newsitem.title: GERMANY: Site for German memorial to Jews now in question.
newsitem.headline: Site for German memorial to Jews now in question.

text.p: In the fractious debate over a planned Berlin memorial to the Nazis' Jewish victims, one of the few earlier points of consensus -- where to erect the monument -- is now in question, officials said on Friday.

Some members of a planners' panel attending the second of three forums on the future of the long-delayed project rejected the proposed site, saying it was the wrong place to honour the memory of the Jews murdered under Hitler.

But the city's top culture official, Peter Radunski, called the reserved plot for the new monument in central Berlin between the Brandenburg Gate and the empty lot where Adolf Hitler's chancellery once stood "an accepted premise".

Berlin architect Bruno Flierl and the authors of an open letter of protest to Radunski suggested a spot near the Platz der Republik square, which faces the Reichstag parliament building, as an alternative.
"The problem with the planned location is that it is not one of real importance to the city," Flierl said. The planned site would lie behind the future British and U.S. embassies.

"It must be a place of vital historical and political meaning for Berliners or it will only be valuable for tourists," Flierl said of what would be the country's first national memorial purely to Jewish Holocaust victims.

The letter's signatories also called for a second design competition to find a replacement for the unpopular 1995 winner, which featured an enormous gravestone engraved with the four and a half million known names of Jewish Nazi victims.

The president of Germany's lower house of parliament, Rita Suessmuth, who was invited to participate in the forum for the day, said all conflicting points of view should be aired before the panel reaches a recommendation.
"I don't wish to attack what those who started this project have already achieved," Suessmuth said. "But we must have an open discussion if we are to reach our goal of consensus."
Her comments drew fire from some of those who have been closely involved with the project for many years.

"I've taken part in this debate since it began eight years ago," said Ignatz Bubis, head of the Central Council of Jews in Germany. "I find it too easy for people who joined the discussion after we reached our decisions to then tear them apart."
The series of forums was intended to focus debate after the original design competition's winner was slammed by Chancellor Helmut Kohl and prominent members of the Jewish community.
But only the 15 million mark ($11 million) budget and the goal of a groundbreaking on January 27, 1999 have remained uncontroversial since the panel's first meeting in January.
The panel of 70 historians, artists, politicians and community leaders plans to meet once more in April before making its final recommendations.
